newsitem.title: CHINA: Japan pledges aid in move to boost China ties.
newsitem.headline: Japan pledges aid in move to boost China ties.

text.p: Japan on Saturday moved to boost battered ties with China by signing an agreement lifting a ban on grant aid and saying it may drop co-sponsorship of a U.N. human rights motion critical of Beijing.

Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda met his Chinese counterpart Qian Qichen in Beijing on Saturday and signed a note for a 1.7 billion yen ($13.7 million) grant for a medical aid project in Nanjing.

Ikeda, who arrived in Beijing on Saturday for two days of talks, also said Tokyo might drop its co-sponsorship of a United Nations motion condemning China's human rights record, Japanese Foreign Ministry spokesman Hidehiko Hamada said.
The two ministers agreed on an exchange of visits between Japanese Prime Minister Ryuarto Hashimoto and Chinese President Jiang Zemin later this year or next year, Hamada said.

The formal agreement to resume the grant aid brought an end to Tokyo's mostly symbolic move to freeze about 7.0 billion yen of aid a year to protest against a Chinese nuclear weapons test in August 1995.

"This is a mark of a symbolic commencement project of the grant aid which has been frozen for almost two years after the nuclear tests conducted by the Chinese government," Hamada told reporters after the meeting.

Ikeda's visit, the first by a senior Japanese official since the death of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping last month, was aimed at thawing out Sino-Japanese ties, strained last by a bitter territorial dispute and a row over Japan's World War Two role.
Ikeda told his hosts Tokyo was reviewing its stance on a motion to censure China at the U.N. Human Rights Commission in Geneva this year, Hamada said.
"Our Foreign Minister said Japan would make further examinations on this issue towards the direction not to be a co-sponsor of the resolution," Hamada said.

The commission, a traditional sparring ground between China and the United States and European nations, had not proven effective in pushing Beijing towards improving its human rights record, Hamada said. Japan has co-sponsored the motion for several years running.
"The fact is almost every year the (European) countries tried this method, but it didn't fly, it was always blocked, only giving the impression that these countries are hostile," Hamada said.

But Ikeda refused to give ground on one of the key irritants in relations last year by repeating Tokyo's claims to a group of disputed East China Sea islands known as the Diaoyus in Chinese and the Senkakus in Japanese. Taiwan also claims the isles.

Tokyo had legal claim to the islands and rejected Beijing's view that they were part of Chinese territory but did not want to see the issue further harm relations, Hamada quoted Ikeda as telling Qian.
"Both sides can agree and would probably share the view that this island issue itself should not jeopardise the already existing friendly and good relations between Japan and China," Hamada said.
The row over the islands flared last year after a right-wing Japanese group built a makeshift lighthouse on one of the islets, triggering violent protests in Taiwan and Hong Kong.
Ties were further chilled by a visit by Hashimoto to a shrine dedicated to Japan's war dead, including World War Two war criminals such as General Hideki Tojo.
Ikeda is scheduled to meet President Jiang and Premier Li Peng on Sunday. ($ = 123.9 Japanese Yen)
